moving_averages.description: Calculate Simple Moving Average (SMA) or Exponential Moving Average (EMA) over defined periods to smooth price data and identify trend direction. When a short-term MA crosses above a long-term MA, it signals bullish momentum; crossover below signals bearish momentum. Professional quants use multiple MA periods (e.g., 50, 100, 200-day) simultaneously to confirm trend strength.
moving_averages.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load commodity price data
df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()

# Calculate Simple Moving Average (SMA)
def calculate_sma(prices, period=20):
    return prices.rolling(window=period).mean()

# Calculate Exponential Moving Average (EMA) - gives more weight to recent prices
def calculate_ema(prices, period=20):
    return prices.ewm(span=period, adjust=False).mean()

# Apply to closing prices
df['SMA_20'] = calculate_sma(df['close'], 20)
df['SMA_50'] = calculate_sma(df['close'], 50)
df['SMA_200'] = calculate_sma(df['close'], 200)
df['EMA_12'] = calculate_ema(df['close'], 12)
df['EMA_26'] = calculate_ema(df['close'], 26)

# Generate trading signals: Buy when short MA crosses above long MA
df['signal'] = 0
df.loc[df['SMA_20'] > df['SMA_200'], 'signal'] = 1  # Bullish
df.loc[df['SMA_20'] < df['SMA_200'], 'signal'] = -1  # Bearish

# Identify crossover points
df['position'] = df['signal'].diff()
buys = df[df['position'] == 2].index  # Crossover from -1 to 1
sells = df[df['position'] == -2].index  # Crossover from 1 to -1

print(f"Number of buy signals: {len(buys)}")
print(f"Number of sell signals: {len(sells)}")

# Visualize
plt.figure(figsize=(14, 6))
plt.plot(df.index, df['close'], label='Close Price', alpha=0.7)
plt.plot(df.index, df['SMA_20'], label='20-day SMA', linewidth=1.5)
plt.plot(df.index, df['SMA_200'], label='200-day SMA', linewidth=1.5)
plt.scatter(buys, df.loc[buys, 'close'], color='green', marker='^', label='Buy Signal')
plt.scatter(sells, df.loc[sells, 'close'], color='red', marker='v', label='Sell Signal')
plt.legend()
plt.title('Moving Average Crossover Strategy')
plt.show()

macd.description: Moving Average Convergence Divergence combines two exponential moving averages (12-period and 26-period) to identify momentum and trend changes. The MACD line is the difference between these EMAs, and a 9-period EMA of the MACD serves as the signal line. When MACD crosses above the signal line, it suggests bullish momentum; crossing below suggests bearish momentum. Histogram (MACD - Signal Line) visually represents this divergence.
macd.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Calculate MACD
def calculate_macd(prices, fast=12, slow=26, signal=9):
    ema_fast = prices.ewm(span=fast, adjust=False).mean()
    ema_slow = prices.ewm(span=slow, adjust=False).mean()
    macd_line = ema_fast - ema_slow
    signal_line = macd_line.ewm(span=signal, adjust=False).mean()
    histogram = macd_line - signal_line
    return macd_line, signal_line, histogram

df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()

df['MACD'], df['Signal'], df['Histogram'] = calculate_macd(df['close'], 12, 26, 9)

# Generate signals: Buy when MACD crosses above signal line
df['MACD_signal'] = 0
df.loc[df['MACD'] > df['Signal'], 'MACD_signal'] = 1  # Bullish
df.loc[df['MACD'] < df['Signal'], 'MACD_signal'] = -1  # Bearish

df['MACD_crossover'] = df['MACD_signal'].diff()
macd_buys = df[df['MACD_crossover'] == 2].index
macd_sells = df[df['MACD_crossover'] == -2].index

# Visualize with two subplots
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(14, 10), sharex=True)

# Price chart
ax1.plot(df.index, df['close'], label='Close Price', color='black', linewidth=2)
ax1.set_ylabel('Price')
ax1.set_title('Commodity Price')
ax1.legend()
ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

# MACD chart
ax2.plot(df.index, df['MACD'], label='MACD', linewidth=1.5, color='blue')
ax2.plot(df.index, df['Signal'], label='Signal Line', linewidth=1.5, color='red')
ax2.bar(df.index, df['Histogram'], label='Histogram', alpha=0.3, color='gray')
ax2.axhline(y=0, color='black', linestyle='-', linewidth=0.5)
ax2.scatter(macd_buys, df.loc[macd_buys, 'MACD'], color='green', marker='^', s=100)
ax2.scatter(macd_sells, df.loc[macd_sells, 'MACD'], color='red', marker='v', s=100)
ax2.set_ylabel('MACD')
ax2.set_title('MACD Indicator')
ax2.legend()
ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

rsi.description: Relative Strength Index measures the magnitude of recent price changes to evaluate overbought or oversold conditions on a scale of 0-100. RSI above 70 typically indicates overbought (potential sell signal), while RSI below 30 indicates oversold (potential buy signal). Calculated using the ratio of average gains to average losses over a period (typically 14 days). Professional quants use RSI divergence: when price makes new highs but RSI doesn't, it signals weakening momentum.
rsi.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def calculate_rsi(prices, period=14):
    # Calculate price changes
    deltas = prices.diff()
    
    # Separate gains and losses
    seed = deltas[:period+1]
    up = seed[seed >= 0].sum() / period
    down = -seed[seed < 0].sum() / period
    
    rs = np.zeros_like(prices)
    rs[:period] = 100. - 100. / (1. + up / down)
    
    for i in range(period, len(prices)):
        delta = deltas.iloc[i]
        if delta > 0:
            upval = delta
            downval = 0.
        else:
            upval = 0.
            downval = -delta
        
        up = (up * (period - 1) + upval) / period
        down = (down * (period - 1) + downval) / period
        rs[i] = 100. - 100. / (1. + up / down)
    
    return pd.Series(rs, index=prices.index)

df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()

df['RSI'] = calculate_rsi(df['close'], period=14)

# Generate signals
df['RSI_signal'] = 0
df.loc[df['RSI'] > 70, 'RSI_signal'] = -1  # Overbought - sell
df.loc[df['RSI'] < 30, 'RSI_signal'] = 1   # Oversold - buy

# Detect RSI divergence: price makes new high but RSI doesn't
df['price_high'] = df['close'].rolling(window=14).max()
df['rsi_high'] = df['RSI'].rolling(window=14).max()
df['bearish_divergence'] = (df['close'] > df['price_high'].shift(1)) & (df['RSI'] < df['rsi_high'].shift(1))

# Visualize
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(14, 10), sharex=True)

ax1.plot(df.index, df['close'], label='Close Price', color='black', linewidth=2)
ax1.set_ylabel('Price')
ax1.set_title('Commodity Price')
ax1.legend()
ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

ax2.plot(df.index, df['RSI'], label='RSI (14)', linewidth=1.5, color='purple')
ax2.axhline(y=70, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, label='Overbought (70)')
ax2.axhline(y=30, color='green', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, label='Oversold (30)')
ax2.fill_between(df.index, 70, 100, alpha=0.2, color='red')
ax2.fill_between(df.index, 0, 30, alpha=0.2, color='green')
ax2.set_ylabel('RSI')
ax2.set_ylim([0, 100])
ax2.set_title('RSI Indicator')
ax2.legend()
ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Bearish divergences detected: {df['bearish_divergence'].sum()}")

bollinger_bands.description: Bollinger Bands consist of a middle band (20-period SMA) and upper/lower bands positioned 2 standard deviations away from the mean. They measure volatility and identify potential breakouts. When price moves outside the bands, it signals potential reversal or continuation depending on context. Narrow bands indicate low volatility; wide bands indicate high volatility. Quants use squeeze setups (narrow bands followed by breakout) to identify high-probability trades.
bollinger_bands.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def calculate_bollinger_bands(prices, period=20, std_dev=2):
    sma = prices.rolling(window=period).mean()
    std = prices.rolling(window=period).std()
    
    upper_band = sma + (std_dev * std)
    lower_band = sma - (std_dev * std)
    
    return upper_band, sma, lower_band

df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()

df['BB_upper'], df['BB_middle'], df['BB_lower'] = calculate_bollinger_bands(df['close'], period=20, std_dev=2)

# Calculate band width and squeeze
df['BB_width'] = df['BB_upper'] - df['BB_lower']
df['BB_width_pct'] = (df['BB_width'] / df['BB_middle']) * 100
df['BB_squeeze'] = df['BB_width_pct'] < df['BB_width_pct'].rolling(window=20).quantile(0.2)

# Identify breakouts
df['above_upper'] = df['close'] > df['BB_upper']
df['below_lower'] = df['close'] < df['BB_lower']

# Generate signals: buy when price bounces off lower band, sell at upper band
df['BB_signal'] = 0
df.loc[df['below_lower'] & (df['close'] > df['close'].shift(1)), 'BB_signal'] = 1   # Buy
df.loc[df['above_upper'] & (df['close'] < df['close'].shift(1)), 'BB_signal'] = -1  # Sell

breakout_buys = df[df['BB_signal'] == 1].index
breakout_sells = df[df['BB_signal'] == -1].index

# Visualize
plt.figure(figsize=(14, 6))
plt.plot(df.index, df['close'], label='Close Price', color='black', linewidth=2)
plt.plot(df.index, df['BB_upper'], label='Upper Band', color='red', linewidth=1, linestyle='--')
plt.plot(df.index, df['BB_middle'], label='20 SMA', color='blue', linewidth=1)
plt.plot(df.index, df['BB_lower'], label='Lower Band', color='green', linewidth=1, linestyle='--')
plt.fill_between(df.index, df['BB_upper'], df['BB_lower'], alpha=0.2, color='gray')
plt.scatter(breakout_buys, df.loc[breakout_buys, 'close'], color='green', marker='^', s=100, label='Buy Signal')
plt.scatter(breakout_sells, df.loc[breakout_sells, 'close'], color='red', marker='v', s=100, label='Sell Signal')
plt.legend()
plt.title('Bollinger Bands Strategy')
plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

print(f"Squeeze setups detected: {df['BB_squeeze'].sum()}")

atr.description: Average True Range measures market volatility by calculating the average of true ranges over a period (typically 14 days). True Range accounts for gaps by taking the maximum of: current high-low, absolute value of high-previous close, absolute value of low-previous close. Professional quants use ATR for dynamic stop-loss placement (e.g., 2*ATR below entry), position sizing, and volatility-based trade filtering. Rising ATR indicates increasing volatility; falling ATR indicates decreasing volatility.
atr.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def calculate_atr(high, low, close, period=14):
    # Calculate True Range
    tr1 = high - low
    tr2 = abs(high - close.shift())
    tr3 = abs(low - close.shift())
    
    # True Range is the maximum of the three
    tr = pd.concat([tr1, tr2, tr3], axis=1).max(axis=1)
    
    # Average True Range using EMA
    atr = tr.ewm(span=period, adjust=False).mean()
    return atr

df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()
df = df[['high', 'low', 'close']]

df['ATR'] = calculate_atr(df['high'], df['low'], df['close'], period=14)

# Use ATR for dynamic stop-loss and position sizing
df['entry_price'] = df['close']  # Assume entry at close
df['stop_loss_2atr'] = df['entry_price'] - (2 * df['ATR'])  # Stop 2*ATR below entry
df['stop_loss_1atr'] = df['entry_price'] - (1 * df['ATR'])  # Stop 1*ATR below entry
df['take_profit_2atr'] = df['entry_price'] + (2 * df['ATR'])  # Take profit 2*ATR above entry

# Risk-reward ratio calculation
df['risk'] = df['entry_price'] - df['stop_loss_2atr']
df['reward'] = df['take_profit_2atr'] - df['entry_price']
df['risk_reward_ratio'] = df['reward'] / df['risk']

# Position size based on risk (assuming 1% risk per trade)
df['position_size_pct'] = (0.01 / df['ATR']) * 100  # Adjust for position sizing

# Visualize
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(14, 10), sharex=True)

# Price with stop-loss and take-profit
ax1.plot(df.index, df['close'], label='Close Price', color='black', linewidth=2)
ax1.fill_between(df.index, df['close'], df['stop_loss_2atr'], alpha=0.2, color='red', label='Risk Zone')
ax1.fill_between(df.index, df['close'], df['take_profit_2atr'], alpha=0.2, color='green', label='Reward Zone')
ax1.plot(df.index, df['stop_loss_2atr'], 'r--', linewidth=1, label='Stop Loss (2*ATR)')
ax1.plot(df.index, df['take_profit_2atr'], 'g--', linewidth=1, label='Take Profit (2*ATR)')
ax1.set_ylabel('Price')
ax1.set_title('ATR-Based Risk Management')
ax1.legend()
ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

# ATR volatility
ax2.plot(df.index, df['ATR'], label='ATR (14)', color='orange', linewidth=2)
ax2.set_ylabel('ATR Value')
ax2.set_title('Volatility Measurement')
ax2.legend()
ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Average Risk-Reward Ratio: {df['risk_reward_ratio'].mean():.2f}")

zscore_normalization.description: Z-score normalization converts price deviations into standard deviation units: (price - mean) / std_dev. Prices beyond ±2 standard deviations indicate extreme moves (95% of normal distribution). Z-score > 2 or < -2 suggests overbought/oversold extremes. Professional quants use z-scores to identify statistical anomalies, mean-reversion setups, and for comparison across different commodities with different scales. Z-scores close to zero indicate mean-reverting behavior.
zscore_normalization.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

def calculate_zscore(prices, period=20):
    # Calculate rolling mean and standard deviation
    rolling_mean = prices.rolling(window=period).mean()
    rolling_std = prices.rolling(window=period).std()
    
    # Calculate Z-score
    zscore = (prices - rolling_mean) / rolling_std
    return zscore

df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()

# Calculate Z-score for commodity price
df['zscore'] = calculate_zscore(df['close'], period=20)

# Generate mean-reversion signals
df['zscore_signal'] = 0
df.loc[df['zscore'] > 2, 'zscore_signal'] = -1    # Extreme overbought - potential sell
df.loc[df['zscore'] < -2, 'zscore_signal'] = 1    # Extreme oversold - potential buy
df.loc[(df['zscore'] > 1) & (df['zscore'] < 2), 'zscore_signal'] = -0.5  # Mild overbought
df.loc[(df['zscore'] < -1) & (df['zscore'] > -2), 'zscore_signal'] = 0.5  # Mild oversold

# Detect mean-reversion entry points: price > 2 std and starting to revert
df['price_derivative'] = df['close'].diff()
df['mean_reversion_buy'] = (df['zscore'] < -2) & (df['price_derivative'] > 0)  # Oversold and rising
df['mean_reversion_sell'] = (df['zscore'] > 2) & (df['price_derivative'] < 0)  # Overbought and falling

mr_buys = df[df['mean_reversion_buy']].index
mr_sells = df[df['mean_reversion_sell']].index

# Calculate mean-reversion strength
rolling_mean = df['close'].rolling(window=20).mean()
df['distance_from_mean_pct'] = ((df['close'] - rolling_mean) / rolling_mean) * 100

# Visualize
fig, (ax1, ax2, ax3) = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(14, 12), sharex=True)

# Price chart
ax1.plot(df.index, df['close'], label='Close Price', color='black', linewidth=2)
ax1.plot(df.index, rolling_mean, label='20-period Mean', color='blue', linewidth=1.5, linestyle='--')
ax1.fill_between(df.index, rolling_mean - 2*df['close'].rolling(20).std(), 
                  rolling_mean + 2*df['close'].rolling(20).std(), alpha=0.2, color='gray', label='±2 Std Dev')
ax1.scatter(mr_buys, df.loc[mr_buys, 'close'], color='green', marker='^', s=100, label='Mean Reversion Buy')
ax1.scatter(mr_sells, df.loc[mr_sells, 'close'], color='red', marker='v', s=100, label='Mean Reversion Sell')
ax1.set_ylabel('Price')
ax1.set_title('Price with Mean Levels')
ax1.legend()
ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

# Z-score chart
ax2.plot(df.index, df['zscore'], label='Z-Score', color='purple', linewidth=1.5)
ax2.axhline(y=2, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, label='Overbought (+2σ)')
ax2.axhline(y=-2, color='green', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, label='Oversold (-2σ)')
ax2.axhline(y=0, color='black', linestyle='-', linewidth=0.5)
ax2.fill_between(df.index, 2, 3, alpha=0.2, color='red')
ax2.fill_between(df.index, -3, -2, alpha=0.2, color='green')
ax2.set_ylabel('Z-Score')
ax2.set_ylim([-4, 4])
ax2.set_title('Z-Score Normalization')
ax2.legend()
ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

# Distance from mean
ax3.bar(df.index, df['distance_from_mean_pct'], label='% Distance from Mean', alpha=0.7, color='steelblue')
ax3.axhline(y=0, color='black', linestyle='-', linewidth=0.5)
ax3.set_ylabel('Distance from Mean (%)')
ax3.set_title('Mean Reversion Distance')
ax3.legend()
ax3.grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Mean Reversion Buy Signals: {len(mr_buys)}")
print(f"Mean Reversion Sell Signals: {len(mr_sells)}")

max_drawdown_sharpe_ratio.description: Maximum Drawdown measures the largest peak-to-trough decline in cumulative returns, representing worst-case loss scenario. Critical for portfolio risk management and position sizing. Sharpe Ratio (return - risk_free_rate) / volatility measures risk-adjusted returns. A Sharpe ratio > 2 indicates excellent risk-adjusted performance; < 1 indicates poor performance. Professional quants use these together: high Sharpe with low max drawdown indicates robust strategy.
max_drawdown_sharpe_ratio.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def calculate_max_drawdown(returns):
    cumsum = (1 + returns).cumprod()
    running_max = cumsum.expanding().max()
    drawdown = (cumsum - running_max) / running_max
    max_dd = drawdown.min()
    return max_dd, drawdown

def calculate_sharpe_ratio(returns, risk_free_rate=0.04, periods_per_year=252):
    # Convert risk-free rate to daily
    daily_rf = (1 + risk_free_rate) ** (1/periods_per_year) - 1
    excess_returns = returns - daily_rf
    sharpe = (excess_returns.mean() / excess_returns.std()) * np.sqrt(periods_per_year)
    return sharpe

df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()

# Calculate daily returns
df['returns'] = df['close'].pct_change()

# Calculate cumulative returns
df['cumulative_returns'] = (1 + df['returns']).cumprod() - 1

# Calculate max drawdown
max_dd, df['drawdown'] = calculate_max_drawdown(df['returns'])

# Calculate Sharpe Ratio
sharpe = calculate_sharpe_ratio(df['returns'], risk_free_rate=0.04)

# Calculate rolling Sharpe (252-day window)
df['rolling_returns_252d'] = df['returns'].rolling(window=252).mean() * 252  # Annualized
df['rolling_volatility_252d'] = df['returns'].rolling(window=252).std() * np.sqrt(252)  # Annualized
df['rolling_sharpe_252d'] = df['rolling_returns_252d'] / df['rolling_volatility_252d']

# Calculate Calmar Ratio (annual return / max drawdown)
annual_return = df['returns'].mean() * 252
df['calmar_ratio'] = annual_return / abs(max_dd)

# Identify periods with recovery from drawdown
df['in_drawdown'] = df['drawdown'] < -0.05  # Significant drawdown (>5%)
df['recovery_period'] = df['drawdown'].diff() > 0  # Start of recovery

recovery_signals = df[df['recovery_period'] & df['in_drawdown'].shift(1)].index

# Visualize
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(14, 12))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(4, 1, hspace=0.3)

# Cumulative returns
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])
ax1.plot(df.index, df['cumulative_returns'] * 100, label='Cumulative Returns', color='black', linewidth=2)
ax1.fill_between(df.index, df['cumulative_returns'] * 100, 0, alpha=0.3, color='green')
ax1.set_ylabel('Cumulative Returns (%)')
ax1.set_title('Cumulative Returns Analysis')
ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax1.legend()

# Drawdown chart
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
ax2.fill_between(df.index, df['drawdown'] * 100, 0, alpha=0.5, color='red', label='Drawdown')
ax2.plot(df.index, df['drawdown'] * 100, color='darkred', linewidth=1.5)
ax2.axhline(y=max_dd * 100, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=2, label=f'Max Drawdown: {max_dd*100:.2f}%')
ax2.set_ylabel('Drawdown (%)')
ax2.set_title('Maximum Drawdown Analysis')
ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax2.legend()

# Rolling Sharpe Ratio
ax3 = fig.add_subplot(gs[2])
ax3.plot(df.index, df['rolling_sharpe_252d'], label='Rolling Sharpe (252d)', color='blue', linewidth=1.5)
ax3.axhline(y=2, color='green', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, label='Excellent (>2)')
ax3.axhline(y=1, color='orange', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, label='Good (1-2)')
ax3.axhline(y=0, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, label='Poor (<0)')
ax3.fill_between(df.index, 2, 3, alpha=0.1, color='green')
ax3.set_ylabel('Sharpe Ratio')
ax3.set_title('Rolling Sharpe Ratio (252-day window)')
ax3.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax3.legend()

# Daily returns histogram
ax4 = fig.add_subplot(gs[3])
ax4.hist(df['returns'].dropna() * 100, bins=100, color='steelblue', alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black')
ax4.axvline(x=df['returns'].mean() * 100, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=2, label=f'Mean: {df["returns"].mean()*100:.3f}%')
ax4.axvline(x=0, color='black', linestyle='-', linewidth=0.5)
ax4.set_xlabel('Daily Returns (%)')
ax4.set_ylabel('Frequency')
ax4.set_title('Distribution of Daily Returns')
ax4.grid(alpha=0.3, axis='y')
ax4.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"\nPerformance Metrics:")
print(f"Max Drawdown: {max_dd*100:.2f}%")
print(f"Sharpe Ratio: {sharpe:.2f}")
print(f"Calmar Ratio: {df['calmar_ratio'].iloc[-1]:.2f}")
print(f"Annual Return: {annual_return*100:.2f}%")
print(f"Annual Volatility: {df['returns'].std()*np.sqrt(252)*100:.2f}%")

mean_reversion.description: Mean reversion strategy exploits the hypothesis that prices fluctuate around a long-term average and extreme deviations will revert. Identifies the historical mean (SMA, EMA) and generates buy signals when price falls below mean (oversold), sell signals when above mean (overbought). Effective for range-bound commodities with strong mean-reverting properties. Uses statistical tests (Augmented Dickey-Fuller, Hurst Exponent) to confirm mean-reversion characteristics before deploying strategy.
mean_reversion.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

def calculate_hurst_exponent(prices, lags_range=range(2, 50)):
    """Calculate Hurst Exponent to determine if series is mean-reverting (H<0.5), random (H≈0.5), or trending (H>0.5)"""
    tau = []
    for lag in lags_range:
        price_diff = prices.diff(lag)
        tau.append(np.sqrt(np.mean(price_diff**2)))
    
    tau = np.array(tau)
    poly = np.polyfit(np.log(lags_range), np.log(tau), 1)
    hurst = poly[0] * 2  # Hurst exponent
    return hurst

def mean_reversion_zscore_strategy(prices, lookback_period=20, entry_threshold=2, exit_threshold=0):
    """
    Strategy: Buy when price is 2 std below mean, sell when reverts to mean.
    Entry_threshold=2 means 2 standard deviations
    """
    rolling_mean = prices.rolling(window=lookback_period).mean()
    rolling_std = prices.rolling(window=lookback_period).std()
    
    zscore = (prices - rolling_mean) / rolling_std
    
    signals = pd.Series(index=prices.index, dtype=float)
    signals[:] = 0
    signals.loc[zscore <= -entry_threshold] = 1      # Buy signal
    signals.loc[zscore >= exit_threshold] = -1       # Sell signal
    
    return signals, zscore, rolling_mean, rolling_std

df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()

# Calculate Hurst Exponent to confirm mean reversion
hurst = calculate_hurst_exponent(df['close'], lags_range=range(2, 50))
print(f"Hurst Exponent: {hurst:.3f}")
if hurst < 0.5:
    print("Series exhibits mean-reverting behavior (good for mean reversion strategy)")
elif hurst > 0.5:
    print("Series exhibits trending behavior (better for trend-following)")
else:
    print("Series exhibits random walk behavior")

# Generate mean reversion signals
signals, zscore, mean, std = mean_reversion_zscore_strategy(df['close'], lookback_period=20, entry_threshold=2)
df['mr_signal'] = signals
df['zscore'] = zscore

df['lower_band'] = mean - 2*std

# Track positions

df['cumulative_buy_hold'] = (1 + df['close'].pct_change()).cumprod() - 1

# Visualize
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(14, 12), sharex=True)

kelly_criterion.description: Kelly Criterion determines optimal position sizing by maximizing long-term wealth growth. Formula: f* = (bp - q) / b, where p=win probability, q=1-p loss probability, b=win/loss ratio. For a 60% win rate with 1:1 payoff ratio, Kelly suggests risking 20% of capital per trade. Professional quants use fractional Kelly (0.25x) for conservative sizing to account for estimation errors and avoid ruin.
kelly_criterion.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def calculate_kelly_fraction(win_rate, avg_win, avg_loss, kelly_fraction=1.0):
    """
    Calculate optimal position size using Kelly Criterion.
    kelly_fraction: Use 0.25 for conservative 1/4 Kelly, 0.5 for half Kelly
    """
    if avg_loss == 0:
        return 0
    
    # f* = (bp - q) / b where b = avg_win/avg_loss, p = win_rate, q = 1-win_rate
    win_loss_ratio = avg_win / avg_loss
    kelly_pct = (win_rate * win_loss_ratio - (1 - win_rate)) / win_loss_ratio
    
    # Apply kelly fraction for safety
    optimal_pct = kelly_pct * kelly_fraction
    
    # Ensure it's between 0 and 1
    return max(0, min(1, optimal_pct))

df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()

# Assume we have a simple trading strategy with entry/exit signals
# Calculate trade outcomes
df['returns'] = df['close'].pct_change()

# Simple signal: buy on RSI < 30, sell on RSI > 70
def calculate_rsi(prices, period=14):
    deltas = prices.diff()
    seed = deltas[:period+1]
    up = seed[seed >= 0].sum() / period
    down = -seed[seed < 0].sum() / period
    rs = np.zeros_like(prices)
    rs[:period] = 100. - 100. / (1. + up / down) if down != 0 else 50
    for i in range(period, len(prices)):
        delta = deltas.iloc[i]
        upval = delta if delta > 0 else 0
        downval = -delta if delta < 0 else 0
        up = (up * (period - 1) + upval) / period
        down = (down * (period - 1) + downval) / period
        rs[i] = 100. - 100. / (1. + up / down) if down != 0 else 50
    return rs

df['rsi'] = calculate_rsi(df['close'], 14)
df['signal'] = 0
df.loc[df['rsi'] < 30, 'signal'] = 1  # Buy
df.loc[df['rsi'] > 70, 'signal'] = -1  # Sell

# Extract trades from signals
trades = []
position = 0
entry_price = 0
for i in range(len(df)):
    if df['signal'].iloc[i] == 1 and position == 0:
        position = 1
        entry_price = df['close'].iloc[i]
    elif df['signal'].iloc[i] == -1 and position == 1:
        exit_price = df['close'].iloc[i]
        pnl_pct = (exit_price - entry_price) / entry_price
        trades.append({
            'entry_price': entry_price,
            'exit_price': exit_price,
            'pnl_pct': pnl_pct,
            'win': pnl_pct > 0
        })
        position = 0

if len(trades) > 0:
    trades_df = pd.DataFrame(trades)
    
    # Calculate Kelly Criterion parameters
    win_rate = trades_df['win'].sum() / len(trades_df)
    winning_trades = trades_df[trades_df['win']]['pnl_pct']
    losing_trades = trades_df[~trades_df['win']]['pnl_pct']
    
    avg_win = winning_trades.mean() if len(winning_trades) > 0 else 0
    avg_loss = abs(losing_trades.mean()) if len(losing_trades) > 0 else 0
    
    # Calculate Kelly percentages
    kelly_full = calculate_kelly_fraction(win_rate, avg_win, avg_loss, kelly_fraction=1.0)
    kelly_half = calculate_kelly_fraction(win_rate, avg_win, avg_loss, kelly_fraction=0.5)
    kelly_quarter = calculate_kelly_fraction(win_rate, avg_win, avg_loss, kelly_fraction=0.25)
    
    print(f"\nTrading Statistics:")
    print(f"Total Trades: {len(trades_df)}")
    print(f"Win Rate: {win_rate*100:.1f}%")
    print(f"Average Win: {avg_win*100:.2f}%")
    print(f"Average Loss: {avg_loss*100:.2f}%")
    print(f"Win/Loss Ratio: {avg_win/avg_loss if avg_loss > 0 else 0:.2f}")
    
    print(f"\nKelly Criterion Results:")
    print(f"Full Kelly (1.0x): {kelly_full*100:.2f}% of capital")
    print(f"Half Kelly (0.5x): {kelly_half*100:.2f}% of capital")
    print(f"Quarter Kelly (0.25x): {kelly_quarter*100:.2f}% of capital (Recommended)")
    
    # Simulate portfolio growth with different Kelly fractions
    capital = 1.0
    kelly_fractions = [kelly_full, kelly_half, kelly_quarter]
    kelly_labels = ['Full Kelly', 'Half Kelly', 'Quarter Kelly']
    
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6))
    
    # Trade outcomes distribution
    ax1.hist(trades_df['pnl_pct'] * 100, bins=30, edgecolor='black', alpha=0.7)
    ax1.axvline(x=avg_win*100, color='green', linestyle='--', label=f'Avg Win: {avg_win*100:.2f}%')
    ax1.axvline(x=-avg_loss*100, color='red', linestyle='--', label=f'Avg Loss: {-avg_loss*100:.2f}%')
    ax1.set_xlabel('Trade P&L (%)')
    ax1.set_ylabel('Frequency')
    ax1.set_title('Distribution of Trade Outcomes')
    ax1.legend()
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)
    
    # Portfolio growth with different Kelly fractions
    colors = ['green', 'blue', 'orange']
    for kelly_frac, label, color in zip(kelly_fractions, kelly_labels, colors):
        capital_series = [1.0]
        for trade in trades:
            capital_series.append(capital_series[-1] * (1 + trade['pnl_pct'] * kelly_frac))
        ax2.plot(capital_series, label=f"{label}: {kelly_frac*100:.1f}%", linewidth=2, color=color)
    
    ax2.set_xlabel('Trade Number')
    ax2.set_ylabel('Portfolio Value (Initial = 1.0)')
    ax2.set_title('Portfolio Growth with Different Kelly Fractions')
    ax2.legend()
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

correlation_cointegration.description: Correlation measures linear relationship between two commodities (-1 to 1 scale). High correlation (>0.7) suggests commodities move together; negative correlation (<-0.3) suggests inverse movement. Cointegration tests whether non-stationary series have long-term equilibrium relationship, critical for pairs trading. Professional quants use correlation heatmaps to identify diversification opportunities and detect structural breaks in relationships.
correlation_cointegration.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import pearsonr, spearmanr
import seaborn as sns
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint, adfuller

# Load multiple commodity price series
df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices_multi.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()
# Assume columns: 'crude_oil', 'natural_gas', 'gold', 'copper', 'wheat'

# Calculate rolling correlation between pairs
def calculate_rolling_correlation(series1, series2, window=60):
    return pd.Series(
        [series1.iloc[i:i+window].corr(series2.iloc[i:i+window]) 
         for i in range(len(series1)-window)],
        index=series1.index[window:]
    )

# Pearson correlation (linear relationship)
corr_matrix = df.corr(method='pearson')
spearman_matrix = df.corr(method='spearman')

print("Pearson Correlation Matrix:")
print(corr_matrix)
print("\nSpearman Correlation Matrix (rank-based):")
print(spearman_matrix)

# Test for cointegration between commodity pairs
def test_cointegration(series1, series2):
    """
    Perform Johansen cointegration test.
    Returns p-value: if < 0.05, series are cointegrated
    """
    score, pvalue, _ = coint(series1, series2)
    return score, pvalue

# Test stationarity (mean reversion indicator)
def test_stationarity(series):
    """
    Augmented Dickey-Fuller test.
    If p-value < 0.05, series is stationary (mean-reverting)
    """
    result = adfuller(series.dropna(), autolag='AIC')
    return result[0], result[1], result[3]  # ADF statistic, p-value, critical values

# Calculate rolling correlation example
if 'crude_oil' in df.columns and 'natural_gas' in df.columns:
    rolling_corr = calculate_rolling_correlation(df['crude_oil'], df['natural_gas'], window=60)
    score, pvalue = test_cointegration(df['crude_oil'].values, df['natural_gas'].values)
    print(f"\nCointegration Test (Crude Oil vs Natural Gas):")
    print(f"Score: {score:.4f}, P-value: {pvalue:.4f}")
    if pvalue < 0.05:
        print("Series are cointegrated (suitable for pairs trading)")
    else:
        print("Series are not cointegrated")

# Visualize correlations
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 12))

# Heatmap of Pearson correlation
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix, annot=True, cmap='RdYlGn', center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, 
            ax=axes[0, 0], fmt='.2f', cbar_kws={'label': 'Correlation'})
axes[0, 0].set_title('Pearson Correlation Heatmap')

# Heatmap of Spearman correlation
sns.heatmap(spearman_matrix, annot=True, cmap='RdYlGn', center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1,
            ax=axes[0, 1], fmt='.2f', cbar_kws={'label': 'Correlation'})
axes[0, 1].set_title('Spearman Correlation Heatmap (Rank-based)')

# Rolling correlation if applicable
if 'crude_oil' in df.columns and 'natural_gas' in df.columns:
    axes[1, 0].plot(rolling_corr.index, rolling_corr.values, label='Rolling Correlation (60-day)', linewidth=2)
    axes[1, 0].axhline(y=0, color='black', linestyle='-', linewidth=0.5)
    axes[1, 0].fill_between(rolling_corr.index, rolling_corr.values, 0, alpha=0.3)
    axes[1, 0].set_ylabel('Correlation')
    axes[1, 0].set_title('Rolling Correlation: Crude Oil vs Natural Gas')
    axes[1, 0].legend()
    axes[1, 0].grid(alpha=0.3)
    axes[1, 0].set_ylim([-1, 1])

# Scatter plot of two correlated commodities
if 'gold' in df.columns and 'copper' in df.columns:
    axes[1, 1].scatter(df['gold'], df['copper'], alpha=0.5, s=10)
    # Add trend line
    z = np.polyfit(df['gold'].dropna(), df['copper'].dropna(), 1)
    p = np.poly1d(z)
    x_trend = np.linspace(df['gold'].min(), df['gold'].max(), 100)
    axes[1, 1].plot(x_trend, p(x_trend), "r--", linewidth=2, label='Trend')
    axes[1, 1].set_xlabel('Gold Price')
    axes[1, 1].set_ylabel('Copper Price')
    axes[1, 1].set_title('Scatter Plot: Gold vs Copper')
    corr_val = df['gold'].corr(df['copper'])
    axes[1, 1].text(0.05, 0.95, f'Correlation: {corr_val:.3f}', 
                    transform=axes[1, 1].transAxes, verticalalignment='top',
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='wheat', alpha=0.5))
    axes[1, 1].legend()
    axes[1, 1].grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Print stationarity tests

for col in df.columns:
    adf_stat, pvalue, crit_vals = test_stationarity(df[col])
    is_stationary = "Yes" if pvalue < 0.05 else "No"

volatility_clustering_garch.description: GARCH (Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity) models capture volatility clustering—periods of high volatility tend to follow high volatility. GARCH(1,1) is standard: variance today depends on yesterday's squared return (shock) and yesterday's variance (persistence). Professional quants use GARCH for volatility forecasting, risk management, and options pricing. Rising beta coefficient indicates stronger volatility persistence.
volatility_clustering_garch.implementation:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from arch import arch_model  # Install: pip install arch

df = pd.read_csv('commodity_prices.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')
df = df.sort_index()

# Calculate daily returns in percentages
df['returns'] = df['close'].pct_change() * 100

# Fit GARCH(1,1) model
garch_model = arch_model(df['returns'].dropna(), vol='Garch', p=1, q=1, rescale=False)
garch_result = garch_model.fit(disp='off')

print("GARCH(1,1) Model Summary:")
print(garch_result.summary())

# Extract volatility components
conditional_volatility = garch_result.conditional_volatility

# Calculate persistence (α + β should be close to 1 for highly persistent volatility)
params = garch_result.params
alpha = params['alpha[1]']
beta = params['beta[1]']
persistence = alpha + beta

print(f"\nVolatility Persistence Analysis:")
print(f"Alpha (shock effect): {alpha:.4f}")
print(f"Beta (persistence): {beta:.4f}")
print(f"Alpha + Beta (persistence): {persistence:.4f}")
if persistence < 1:
    print("Mean-reverting volatility (good for range-bound commodities)")
elif persistence >= 1:
    print("Highly persistent volatility (watch for regime changes)")

# Forecast future volatility
forecast = garch_result.forecast(horizon=20)
forecast_variance = forecast.variance.iloc[-1]
forecast_volatility = np.sqrt(forecast_variance)

# Visualize
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(14, 12), sharex=True)

# Returns
axes[0].bar(df.index, df['returns'], alpha=0.6, label='Daily Returns', color='steelblue')
axes[0].axhline(y=0, color='black', linestyle='-', linewidth=0.5)
axes[0].set_ylabel('Returns (%)')
axes[0].set_title('Daily Returns')
axes[0].legend()
axes[0].grid(alpha=0.3)

# Conditional Volatility from GARCH
axes[1].plot(df.index[1:], conditional_volatility.values, label='GARCH(1,1) Volatility', 
             linewidth=2, color='orange')
axes[1].fill_between(df.index[1:], conditional_volatility.values, alpha=0.3, color='orange')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Volatility (%)')
axes[1].set_title('Conditional Volatility Estimates')
axes[1].legend()
axes[1].grid(alpha=0.3)

# Squared Returns vs Conditional Variance (shows clustering)
axes[2].scatter(df.index, df['returns']**2, alpha=0.5, s=20, label='Squared Returns', color='red')
axes[2].plot(df.index[1:], conditional_volatility.values**2, label='Conditional Variance', 
             linewidth=2, color='blue')
axes[2].set_ylabel('Variance (squared returns)')
axes[2].set_xlabel('Date')
axes[2].set_title('Volatility Clustering: Squared Returns vs GARCH Variance')
axes[2].legend()
axes[2].grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Plot forecast
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))
ax.plot(df.index[-100:], conditional_volatility.values[-100:], label='Historical Volatility', linewidth=2)
future_dates = pd.date_range(start=df.index[-1], periods=21, freq='D')
forecast_plot = [conditional_volatility.values[-1]] + list(np.sqrt(forecast_variance.values[0]))
ax.plot(future_dates, forecast_plot, 'r--', linewidth=2, label='GARCH Forecast (20-day)')
ax.set_ylabel('Volatility (%)')
ax.set_xlabel('Date')
ax.set_title('GARCH(1,1) Volatility Forecast')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
